prompt: In the past, some families in northern Europe covered their houses with turf for protection against the cold.

label_provenance.note: written by an AI agent; not checked by a human

passage:
Cities that grow upward often run short of ground-level space for parks, so some planners have started to look at rooftops instead. A green roof is a roof covered with soil and plants, and the idea is much older than most people assume: families in northern Europe laid turf over their wooden houses centuries ago to keep out the cold. Modern versions are thinner and lighter, built in layers that include a waterproof membrane, a drainage sheet and a shallow growing medium.

The benefits are easiest to see during summer. A conventional dark roof can become far hotter than the surrounding air, whereas a planted roof stays cooler because the plants shade the surface and release water vapour. Buildings below therefore need less air conditioning, and the roof membrane is protected from sunlight, which can double its working life. Green roofs also hold back rainwater. In one study of a mid-sized city, planted roofs delayed the peak of runoff after a storm by about twenty minutes, giving drains more time to cope.

There are drawbacks. A green roof costs more to install than a standard one, and the structure beneath must be strong enough to carry the extra weight of wet soil. Maintenance is also needed, since weeds and dry spells can damage thin plant layers. Supporters argue that these costs are recovered through lower energy bills, although the researchers who carried out the city study did not measure savings over more than five years. Critics point out that a roof garden open to the public raises insurance questions that a sealed roof does not.
evidence: families in northern Europe laid turf over their wooden houses centuries ago to keep out the cold

prompt: Keepers believe that city plants flower at varied times, which helps bees to find food for much of the year.

label_provenance.note: written by an AI agent; not checked by a human

passage:
Beekeeping has moved from the countryside to the city in the last two decades. Hives now sit on office roofs, in school gardens and beside railway lines. Keepers say that cities offer a surprisingly good home because gardens, parks and street trees flower at different times of year, giving bees food from early spring to late autumn.

Urban honey is not always better than rural honey, however. A survey of hives in one large city found that colonies in dense districts produced less honey per hive than those on the edge of town, because rooftop forage was patchy. The same survey recorded that the honey itself contained no more pollutants than honey from farmland. Some ecologists worry that the number of hives has grown faster than the supply of flowers, so that honeybees compete with wild bees for nectar.

Several cities have therefore begun to limit hive numbers in busy parks. Wild bee specialists recommend that anyone who wants to help should plant a variety of flowers rather than keep a hive. Beekeeping groups reply that hives are valuable for education, since many new keepers become more interested in protecting nature in general.
evidence: gardens, parks and street trees flower at different times of year, giving bees food from early spring to late autumn

prompt: Teenagers usually go to sleep later than younger children.

label_provenance.note: written by an AI agent; not checked by a human

passage:
In many countries the school day begins before eight o'clock, even though teenagers tend to fall asleep later than children or adults. Sleep researchers explain that the body clock shifts during adolescence, so a fifteen-year-old who is asked to wake at six may be getting up at the equivalent of a much earlier hour for an adult. Surveys of students show that many of them sleep for fewer than eight hours on school nights.

Several school districts have tested later start times. In one trial involving nine schools, classes began about an hour later than before. Attendance rose slightly, and teachers reported that fewer students fell asleep in the first lesson. The trial did not, however, produce a clear change in examination results, and the authors warned that two years was too short a period for judging academic effects.

Not everyone supports the change. Parents who work early shifts say that a later start leaves their children unsupervised in the morning, while sports coaches point out that afternoon training sessions would end after dark. Bus companies add that rearranging routes costs money. Supporters reply that these problems can be managed, and that the health benefits justify the effort.
evidence: teenagers tend to fall asleep later than children or adults

prompt: Modern ship sails differ in form from traditional canvas sails.

label_provenance.note: written by an AI agent; not checked by a human

passage:
Most of the goods people buy travel at least part of their journey by sea, and the ships that carry them burn large amounts of fuel. A growing number of shipping companies are therefore testing a technology that seems to belong to the past: sails. The modern versions are not canvas but tall rigid wings or spinning cylinders that use the wind to push the ship forward.

Engineers say that the main advantage of these devices is that they can be added to existing vessels. On a long route across an ocean, a ship fitted with rotating cylinders used about one tenth less fuel than a similar ship without them. The saving depends heavily on the route, since a ship sailing against steady winds gains little. Designers have also had to solve the problem of bridges and ports, because tall rigs must fold down or tilt to pass underneath.

Cost remains a barrier. Fuel is cheap compared with the price of a new rig, and many owners wait to see how long the equipment lasts at sea. Some analysts believe that stricter rules on emissions will change this calculation within a decade. Others doubt that sails alone will be enough, and argue that they should be combined with cleaner fuels.
evidence: The modern versions are not canvas but tall rigid wings or spinning cylinders

prompt: Older learners can sometimes make faster early progress than children.

label_provenance.note: written by an AI agent; not checked by a human

passage:
Adults who start learning a new language often assume that children have an unbeatable advantage. Research gives a more mixed picture. Young children do tend to acquire a native-like accent more easily, but older learners can progress faster in the early stages because they understand grammar rules and can study in a planned way.

A study of two hundred immigrants found that the best predictor of fluency after five years was not the age of arrival but the amount of daily conversation in the new language. Those who spent at least two hours a day speaking with local people outperformed those who relied mainly on classes. The researchers suggested that classes work best when they are combined with real conversation.

Technology has made conversation practice easier to find. Language exchange websites connect learners with partners abroad, and some apps offer short speaking tasks. Critics, however, observe that many app users stop within a month, and that games which reward streaks may encourage frequent but shallow practice.
evidence: older learners can progress faster in the early stages
